chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Muhammad ibn Isa from Ubayd from Yunus from Abu Basir and Sama'ah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a group of people who fasted the month of Ramadan, and a black cloud covered them at sunset, so they thought it was night, he said: 'Upon the one who broke his fast is the making up of that day, for indeed Allah, Exalted and Glorious, says, "Then complete the fast until night." So whoever ate before night entered, upon him is its making up, because he ate deliberately.'

The meaning in this narration is that when one doubts the entry of night due to an occurrence (like clouds), and his conjectures are equal and neither has an advantage over the other, it is not permissible for him to break his fast until he is certain of the entry of night or his conjecture prevails. And when he breaks his fast while the state is as described, making up (the fast) is obligatory upon him according to what this report contains. As for when his conjection prevails that night has entered, so he breaks his fast, then it becomes clear afterwards that night had not entered, he should refrain from food and there is no making up upon him. And that which indicates what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.صِيَامُ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمِ: making up the fast of that day

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if I break my fast due to doubt about sunset because of clouds?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* clarifies the juristic principle of *al-ghalab al-zann* (prevailing conjecture) in determining Maghrib, emphasizing that doubt alone does not invalidate the fast unless accompanied by a specific external sign like a black cloud. It establishes that breaking the fast based on strong probability is valid even if later proven incorrect, whereas equal doubt requires waiting for certainty to avoid obligatory *qada* (making up). This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on practical certainty (*yaqin*) over speculative doubt in ritual acts.
